questions.q: According to Postulate 1, what is required of the vector that represents a quantum system's state?
options: It must have only real-number components, never complex ones
It must be a vector in a complex Hilbert space that is normalized — its squared-amplitude length equals 1
It must have exactly two components, regardless of the system
It must be an eigenvalue of a Hermitian operator
questions.explain: Postulate 1 states the full description of a quantum system is a normalized vector in a complex Hilbert space. For a qubit, |ψ⟩ = a|0⟩ + b|1⟩ with |a|²+|b|²=1. Components are generally complex, not restricted to real numbers, and eigenvalues belong to postulate 3, not postulate 1.

questions.q: Why does Postulate 2 specifically require observables to be represented by Hermitian operators rather than arbitrary operators?
options: Hermitian operators are easier to write down in matrix form
Hermitian operators are guaranteed to have only real eigenvalues, which is essential because those eigenvalues are the actual possible outcomes of a measurement
Hermitian operators are always unitary as well
Hermitian operators always have exactly two eigenvalues
questions.explain: A measured physical quantity must come out as a real number. Hermitian operators are mathematically guaranteed to have real eigenvalues, so requiring observables to be Hermitian ensures measurement outcomes (postulate 3's eigenvalues) are always real, never complex.

questions.q: For the verified state |ψ⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩, what does the Born rule give for P(0) and P(1), and why aren't the amplitudes themselves the probabilities?
options: P(0) = 0.6, P(1) = 0.8, because amplitudes directly equal probabilities
P(0) = 0.36, P(1) = 0.64, because the Born rule requires squaring each amplitude's magnitude to get its probability, not using the amplitude directly
P(0) = 0.64, P(1) = 0.36, because probabilities are assigned to the larger amplitude's opposite outcome
P(0) and P(1) cannot be determined without knowing the measurement basis in advance
questions.explain: The Born rule squares each amplitude's magnitude: 0.6²=0.36 for outcome 0, 0.8²=0.64 for outcome 1, summing to 1 as required. Amplitudes (0.6, 0.8) are not themselves probabilities — squaring is the essential step the Born rule adds.

questions.q: According to Postulate 4, if measuring |ψ⟩ = 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩ yields outcome 1, what is the qubit's state immediately after the measurement?
options: It remains 0.6|0⟩ + 0.8|1⟩, unchanged by the measurement
It becomes |1⟩ — the state collapses to the eigenstate matching the outcome obtained, with the |0⟩ component gone entirely
It becomes 0.8|0⟩ + 0.6|1⟩, with the amplitudes swapped
It becomes an equal superposition (|0⟩+|1⟩)/√2
questions.explain: Postulate 4 (collapse) says the state immediately after measurement becomes exactly the eigenstate corresponding to the observed outcome. Getting outcome 1 collapses the state to |1⟩, discarding the superposition entirely, which is why an immediate re-measurement gives 1 with certainty.

questions.q: Why does Postulate 5 (unitary time evolution of closed systems) directly explain why quantum logic gates are represented as unitary matrices?
options: Because unitary matrices are simply easier for classical computers to simulate

Because a quantum gate is a piece of closed-system time evolution, and Postulate 5 requires that closed-system evolution always be represented by a unitary operator, which preserves normalization and is reversible
Because Postulate 5 only applies to measurement, which gates also perform
Because unitary matrices are the only matrices that have real eigenvalues
questions.explain: A gate acting on qubits without measuring them is exactly the kind of closed-system evolution Postulate 5 describes, so it must be unitary: normalization-preserving and reversible. This is the direct bridge between the physics postulate and why every quantum gate you'll encounter later is a unitary matrix.
